name: Weighted blanket
lead: A weighted blanket is a blanket filled with pellets, glass beads or chains so that it presses evenly on the body, commonly weighing about 5 to 30 pounds (2.3 to 13.6 kg).[1][2] It is used in occupational therapy for deep pressure stimulation and is sold to consumers as a sleep and anxiety aid. In sleep-focused communities it is discussed as a way to feel calmer at bedtime.

Published research is limited and mixed. A 2020 systematic review described the literature on weighted blankets as sparse,[3] a randomized trial in psychiatric patients with insomnia reported benefit on an insomnia scale,[4] and a randomized crossover trial in autistic children found no significant change in the main sleep measures.[5] Safety concerns are documented for young children and people with respiratory or circulatory conditions.[1][2]

paras: Weighted blankets distribute weight through stitched pockets or quilted compartments so it does not shift. Plastic-pellet fillings are cheaper but bulkier, while glass or metal fillings are denser and require less bulk.[1] Reference guidance commonly cited is a weight of about 10 percent of the user's body weight.[2]

Temple Grandin built a "hug machine" in the 1960s to study the calming effect of deep touch pressure.[1] Keith and Lynda Zivalich made a bean-filled comforter in 1997 and began selling it in late 1998, and occupational therapist Tina Champagne carried out a first formal study in 1999.[1] Use grew in the special-needs community through the 2000s, and a 2017 crowdfunding campaign for the Gravity Blanket raised nearly $5 million, after which retailers worldwide began stocking weighted blankets.[1]

sections.h: How it is proposed to work
paras: Proponents attribute the effect to deep pressure stimulation, which they say engages the parasympathetic nervous system and is accompanied by changes in serotonin, melatonin and cortisol.[2] This account is a proposed mechanism; reviewers note that research on weighted blankets is sparse and that a placebo effect must be accounted for in future studies.[1][3]
A 2020 systematic review in the American Journal of Occupational Therapy concluded that research on weighted blankets was sparse and that more study was needed on anxiety and insomnia.[3]

A 2014 randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial in children and adolescents with autism and severe sleep problems compared a weighted blanket with an otherwise identical light blanket.[5] A 2020 randomized trial of 120 patients with depression, bipolar disorder, generalized anxiety disorder or ADHD compared a weighted chain blanket with a light plastic chain blanket for four weeks, with the Insomnia Severity Index as the primary outcome; the authors reported greater improvement with the weighted blanket.[4]

A 2024 randomized crossover trial examined weighted blankets for sleep in children with ADHD,[6] and a retrospective follow-up study looked at children and adults with ADHD and/or autism.[7] Small studies in inpatient psychiatric settings have examined anxiety and distress.[8] Most studies involve clinical populations, and evidence in healthy adults seeking better sleep is limited.

Scientists caution that findings in healthy adults do not necessarily apply to children, particularly those with disabilities, and a child's death has been linked to improper use.[1] Manufacturers and clinical guidance commonly state that weighted blankets are not intended for infants or very small children, and suggest that people with respiratory problems such as sleep apnea, or circulatory problems, consult a clinician first.[2]

Weighted blankets appear in the sleep and recovery category as a comfort aid for people who want to fall asleep faster, sometimes alongside cooling bedding and fixed bedtimes. No studies have examined them for appearance outcomes.

card.summary: A heavy blanket for calming pressure at bedtime; trial evidence exists mainly in clinical groups and is mixed.
card.note: Not advised for infants or very small children; people with breathing problems are advised to consult a clinician.

quick.overview:
A weighted blanket is a quilt filled with pellets, beads or chains that presses evenly on the body. It came out of occupational therapy and became a mainstream consumer product after 2017.

Studies are mostly in autistic, ADHD or psychiatric populations and results are mixed; evidence in healthy adults is limited, and nothing tests it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say deep pressure calms the nervous system, in a way similar to being hugged. This remains a proposed mechanism.
quick.risks: Safety warnings concern infants and small children, and people with respiratory or circulatory conditions. A child's death linked to improper use has been reported.
